title.en: Part 3 · How are public spaces changing?

samples.text: Well, in my country, I think the biggest change is that a lot of open space has been replaced by buildings, especially shopping malls and apartment blocks. As cities grow, land becomes very expensive, so developers want to use every piece of it. On the other hand, the government has also built some new parks and walking streets recently, and these are quite popular, especially at weekends. So overall I think the changes are partly positive, but we still need more green space, because many people live in small apartments and they need somewhere to go outside.

samples.text: I'd say there have been two quite contradictory trends. On one hand, a lot of traditional open space, things like markets and empty lots where kids used to play, has disappeared to make way for malls and high-rise flats, so public life has become more commercialised. On the other, local authorities have started to recognise the value of green space, so we're seeing riverside walkways and pedestrian streets that simply didn't exist ten years ago. Overall I think it's a positive direction, but the risk is that the new spaces are mostly in wealthier districts, so not everyone benefits equally.

samples.text: It's been a real mixed bag, I think. For a long stretch, the dominant pattern was that open, informal spaces, street markets, patches of wasteland, even wide pavements, were steadily swallowed up by development, and a lot of social life moved indoors into shopping malls, where you're essentially a customer rather than a citizen. More recently, though, there's been a noticeable push the other way: cities are converting old railway lines into parks or closing streets to traffic at weekends. I'd call that broadly positive, but I'd add one caveat, which is that some of these new spaces are so carefully designed and policed that they feel more like showrooms than genuinely public places. A good public space, to my mind, is one where you can do nothing in particular without being moved on.

samples.text: I think the honest answer is that public space has become both better and narrower. Better, because cities have finally woken up to the idea that people need somewhere to breathe, so you get these lovely riverside promenades and car-free weekends that would have been unthinkable a generation ago. Narrower, because a lot of what's being created is quietly conditional: it's privately managed, there are rules about where you can sit, and the whole thing is designed around a particular kind of visitor, usually one with money to spend in the cafés nearby. So yes, it's largely positive, but I'd judge a city less by how attractive its new plazas look and more by whether a teenager with no money, or an elderly man with nowhere else to go, would feel welcome to spend an afternoon there.
